title: Workflow Security Hardening
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of workflow security hardening and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to workflow security hardening.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on workflow security hardening. Harden workflows with least privilege, isolated trust zones, protected deployment credentials, reviewed action references, safe expressions, and sanitized artifacts. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Workflow Security Hardening matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Harden workflows with least privilege, isolated trust zones, protected deployment credentials, reviewed action references, safe expressions, and sanitized artifacts. Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available.

content_blocks.title: Security trust boundaries
content_blocks.alt_text: Untrusted contribution enters read-only validation, then crosses a review boundary before an isolated protected deployment zone.
content_blocks.caption: Keep untrusted contribution validation separate from credentialed deployment.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Harden workflows with least privilege, isolated trust zones, protected deployment credentials, reviewed action references, safe expressions, and sanitized artifacts. Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Least-privilege token policies
items.text: Declare only the token scopes the job requires. A read-only job should not receive write access; verify permissions at workflow and job scope and review organization policy.

items.title: Protecting deployment credentials
items.text: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

items.title: Separating trusted and untrusted jobs
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Preventing script injection
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Runner isolation
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

items.title: Protecting caches and artifacts
items.text: Cache rebuildable dependencies using a key that includes the package manager, runtime/OS as appropriate, and lockfile hash. A cache miss must not change build correctness, and secrets do not belong in caches.

items.title: Reviewing security-sensitive workflow changes
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Auditing privileged automation
items.text: Record ownership, approval boundaries, version/pin choices, permission policy, and release evidence so another maintainer can explain and audit the automation.

items.title: action usage, OIDC, and the risks of privileged pull-request workflows as distinct concerns.
items.text: Use OIDC only after the cloud trust policy constrains the issuer, audience, repository, ref/environment subject, and role permissions; grant `id-token: write` only to the job that requests the token.

content_blocks.code:
name: Harden a validation workflow
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: validation-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Run non-privileged checks"
content_blocks.expected_output: The workflow uses read-only repository permissions, a bounded timeout, and a concurrency group that cancels outdated validation runs. Review cancellation behavior before applying this pattern to deployments.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the secret/variable scope and permissions match your environment before a real run.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove the temporary workflow and revoke test credentials or app installations when finished.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to workflow security hardening. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain workflow security hardening, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Constrain credentials and token permissions, and prefer scoped, short-lived authentication where supported.

content.task: Apply workflow security hardening to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Harden workflows with least privilege, isolated trust zones, protected deployment credentials, reviewed action references, safe expressions, and sanitized artifacts.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.

content.expected_output: The workflow uses read-only repository permissions, a bounded timeout, and a concurrency group that cancels outdated validation runs. Review cancellation behavior before applying this pattern to deployments.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.

Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
